subject: Architecture
title: Art Nouveau: When Buildings Grew Vines
description: Learn Art Nouveau: When Buildings Grew Vines in one minute.

hook.text: Around 1890, architects decided buildings should look like nature — curves, vines, and flowers.

buildup.text: Art Nouveau rejected straight lines. Iron was bent into whiplash curves mimicking plant stems.

discovery.text: Hector Guimard's Paris Métro entrances look like giant iron plants growing from the sidewalk.

twist.text: Every piece was custom-made. Mass production killed the style because it was too expensive.

climax.text: Antoni Gaudí pushed Art Nouveau furthest — his buildings in Barcelona look almost alive.

punchline.text: They built nature from iron and glass. Then the factories made it extinct.

quiz.question: What ultimately killed the Art Nouveau movement?
options: A shift in public taste toward classical styles
Custom craftsmanship was too expensive for mass production

details.summary: Art Nouveau rejected industrial uniformity in favor of organic forms inspired by plants, flowing lines, and handcraft. Flourishing from the 1890s to 1910, it produced masterpieces by Gaudí, Horta, and Guimard that made buildings look as if they had grown rather than been constructed.
details.whyItMatters: Art Nouveau was the first truly modern style that rejected historical copying. Its insistence on organic form and integrated design influenced Art Deco, mid-century modernism, and today's biomorphic architecture.
takeaways: Art Nouveau used organic, plant-inspired forms and flowing lines
It flourished from the 1890s to 1910 as a reaction to industry
Gaudí, Horta, and Guimard were its leading architects

faq.question: Why did Art Nouveau disappear so quickly?
faq.answer: Its handcrafted ornament was expensive and slow to produce, making it impractical for widespread use. World War I also killed the optimistic spirit that nurtured it. Modernism's machine aesthetic replaced organic curves with geometric efficiency.

faq.question: Where can you see Art Nouveau architecture?
faq.answer: Brussels (Victor Horta's townhouses), Barcelona (Gaudí's Casa Batlló and Park Güell), Paris (Hector Guimard's Metro entrances), and Riga, Latvia (which has Europe's largest concentration of Art Nouveau buildings — over 800 in the city center).
